To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of developing colon and rectum cancers after cervical cancer treatment is higher for women who received radiation than for those who did not, and the risk of colon and/or rectum cancer after radiation treatment is similar across the three eras of treatment.
the risk of colon and/or rectal cancer is increased among cervical cancer survivors who received radiation treatment, and this risk remains the same across three different time periods.
radiation therapy is associated with increased risk of colon and, especially, rectal cancer after 8 years of followup.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a long-term risk of developing colorectal cancer in women with cervical cancer.
the risk of developing colorectal cancer in cervical cancer survivors who received radiation treatment.
the risk of colorectal cancer in long-term survivors of cervical cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radiation-induced second cancers of colon and rectal cancer occur 8  years after radiation treatment for cervix cancer.
the risk of colon and/or rectal cancer is higher among long-term cervical survivors who received XRT.
radiation-induced colon and rectum cancers may occur after 8 years of treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radiation therapy for cervical cancer increases the risk of developing colon and rectum cancers, especially after 8 years of radiation.
the risk of colon and especially rectum cancer after radiation treatment for cervix cancer may be higher than previously thought.   1
radiation-induced second cancers of colon and rectal may occur 15 years after radiation therapy for cervical cancer.   1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radiation treatment for cervical carcinoma increases the risk of developing colorectal cancer.
the risk of developing colon and rectum cancers after 35 years is substantial.
women with cervical cancer who received radiation treatment have an increased risk of developing second cancers of the colorectum.
